content: Mouth sores can develop in various areas of the oral cavity, including the inner cheeks, gums, tongue, lips, or palate. These sores can arise from different causes and present in various forms. Causes of Mouth Sores: 1. Cold Sores (Fever Blisters): These are caused by the herpes simplex virus and are highly contagious. Symptoms often begin with tenderness, tingling, or a burning sensation before the sore appears. Cold sores typically start as blisters and then form a crust. The herpes virus can remain dormant in the body for years and may be triggered by factors such as: Another illness, especially with fever. Hormonal changes, such as during menstruation. Stress. Sun exposure. 2. Canker Sores: These are not contagious. They may appear as a single pale or yellow ulcer with a red border or as a cluster of such sores. The exact cause is unclear but may be linked to: Viral infections. Temporary immune system weakness (e.g., from a cold or flu). Hormonal changes. Irritation. Stress. Deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folate. 3. Other Irritations: Sharp or broken teeth, or poorly fitting dentures. Biting the cheek, tongue, or lip. Burns from hot food or drinks. Braces. Chewing tobacco. 4. Less Common Causes: Mouth sores may indicate underlying conditions such as: Autoimmune disorders (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus). Bleeding disorders. Cancer. Infections (e.g., hand-foot-mouth disease). A weakened immune system (e.g., due to AIDS or post-transplant medications). 5. Medications That May Cause Mouth Sores: Aspirin. Barbiturates (used for insomnia). Chemotherapy drugs. Gold (used for rheumatoid arthritis). Penicillin. Phenytoin (used for seizures). Streptomycin. Sulfonamides. Risk Factors: Women are more prone to canker sores than men, possibly due to hormonal changes. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if: A sore develops shortly after starting a new medication. Large white patches appear on the roof of the mouth or tongue (this may indicate thrush or another infection). A mouth sore persists for more than two weeks. You have a weakened immune system (e.g., from HIV or cancer). Other symptoms accompany the sore, such as fever, skin rash, drooling, or difficulty swallowing. Treatment Options: Most mouth sores resolve within 10 to 14 days without treatment, though some may last up to six weeks. To alleviate discomfort: Avoid hot beverages, spicy or salty foods, and citrus. Gargle with cool water or consume popsicles, especially for burns. Use over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen. For canker sores: Rinse with salt water. Apply a paste made of baking soda and water. Use a mixture of hydrogen peroxide and water (1:1 ratio) applied with a cotton swab. Severe cases may require treatments like fluocinonide gel (Lidex), anti-inflammatory amlexanox paste (Aphthasol), or chlorhexidine gluconate (Peridex) mouthwash. Nonprescription products like Orabase can protect sores inside the lips or on the gums. Blistex or Campho-Phenique may provide relief for canker sores and fever blisters, especially if applied early. For cold sores: Applying ice to the sore may help. Antiviral medications may be prescribed, though their effectiveness in shortening the duration of sores is debated. Prevention: To reduce the risk of common mouth sores: Avoid very hot foods or beverages. Manage stress and practice relaxation techniques like yoga or meditation. To prevent irritation: Chew food slowly. Use a soft-bristle toothbrush. Address dental issues like sharp teeth or poorly fitting dentures promptly. For frequent canker sores, consult a doctor about taking folate and vitamin B12 supplements. To prevent the spread of herpes sores: Avoid kissing or oral sex with someone who has an active cold sore. Refrain from these activities when you have an active sore. Do not share razors, lip balm, toothbrushes, or lipsticks. To prevent cancerous mouth sores: Avoid smoking or using tobacco. Limit alcohol consumption to two drinks per day. Protect your lips with a wide-brimmed hat and lip balm containing SPF 15. Medical Evaluation: A doctor will perform a physical examination, focusing on the mouth and tongue, and may ask questions such as: Where are the sores located (e.g., lips, gums, tongue, cheeks)? Are the sores open ulcers? Are there large white patches on the roof of the mouth or tongue? How long have the sores been present? Have you had similar sores before? What medications are you taking? Are there other symptoms like fever, sore throat, or bad breath? Treatment Based on Cause: Topical anesthetics like lidocaine or xylocaine may relieve pain but should be avoided in children. Antifungal medications may be prescribed for oral thrush. Antiviral medications may be used for herpes sores, though their efficacy is debated. Anti-inflammatory medications may be prescribed for severe or persistent canker sores.
